The test image shows a close-up microscopic view of a stem/plant tissue with:
- Dense gray-brown velvety sporulation with individual stalked spore structures (conidiophores)
- A dark black mass in the upper right (possible sclerotium)
- White/silvery underlying tissue

This pattern strongly suggests Gray Mold (Botrytis) or possibly Rhizopus. Let me check reference images.

The Gray Mold Bugwood_15 is a microscopic view of Botrytis conidia (Bruce Watt photographer, same as test image). The test image also shows dense gray-brown sporulation on stem tissue. Let me check Rhizopus and Alternaria for comparison.

Having used all 8 reference image views, here is my analysis:

**Test image key features:**
- Close-up microscopic view of stem/plant tissue edge
- Dense gray-brown velvety sporulation with individual conidiophore stalks and rounded spores at tips
- Dark black mass in upper right (consistent with a sclerotium)
- White/silvery underlying plant tissue
- Photographed by Bruce Watt (same photographer as Gray Mold Bugwood_15)

**Reference comparison:**
- **Gray Mold (Bugwood_15)**: Also by Bruce Watt, shows Botrytis conidia as round spores on branching conidiophores. The test image is a lower-magnification view showing the same type of sporulation massed on stem tissue. Description matches: "dense velvety gray-brown spore mass; spores light brown-gray on black stalks."
- **Rhizopus**: Shows fibrous/stringy mycelia, not individual stalked spores — does not match.
- **Alternaria**: Shows segmented, hand-grenade-shaped conidia — completely different morphology.
- **Sclerotinia**: White cottony mycelium with developing sclerotia — different texture and color.
- **Powdery Mildew / Southern Blight**: Clearly different appearances.

The test image visually matches Gray Mold most closely — the individual stalked gray-brown conidia, the velvety texture, and the dark black sclerotium-like mass are all hallmarks of Botrytis cinerea.
